main_point: Aaron Swartz, an open source programmer and Harvard fellow, has been arrested and charged with multiple computer crimes for downloading millions of copyrighted academic articles from JSTOR, an act that has sparked debate over copyright enforcement and digital access to knowledge.

statements.text: Aaron Swartz, a Harvard fellow and open source programmer, has been arrested and charged with multiple computer crimes for downloading millions of copyrighted academic articles from JSTOR, an act that has sparked debate over copyright enforcement and digital access to knowledge.
statements.text_short: Aaron Swartz faces arrest for downloading millions of copyrighted academic articles from JSTOR.

statements.text: JSTOR intends not to pursue civil litigation against Aaron Swartz, despite his indictment by the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts for downloading millions of copyrighted academic articles, signaling a strategic choice to avoid further legal escalation while the criminal case proceeds.
statements.text_short: JSTOR will not file a civil lawsuit against Aaron Swartz.

statements.text: Aaron Swartz was arrested for downloading millions of copyrighted academic articles from JSTOR. He pleaded not guilty to all charges, which included wire fraud and computer fraud. He was released on a $100,000 unsecured bond.
statements.text_short: Aaron Swartz entered a not guilty plea and was freed on an unsecured bond worth $100,000.

statements.text: Greg Maxwell, who contributes to Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons, uploaded a torrent to The Pirate Bay. This file holds 33 gigabytes of documents from the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society. These papers are public domain in the United States, yet JSTOR previously sold them for a fee. This situation mirrors the legal and ethical issues found in Swartz's case.
statements.text_short: Greg Maxwell published a torrent of public domain Royal Society papers previously sold by JSTOR.
